Micro-scale spatial metagenomics | Practical AlberdiLab · 3D’omics 2026-09-02 Chapter 1 Introduction Conventional metagenomics grinds up a whole gut sample and asks which bacteria live in this animal. It cannot ask where they live, because the moment the sample is homogenised all spatial information is gone. Micro-scale spatial metagenomics (MSSM) keeps that information. A frozen section of intestinal tissue is photographed, and a laser cuts out hundreds of tiny pieces — microsamples — each only a few hundred micrometres across. Each microsample is sequenced separately, and because the laser recorded where it cut, every community profile comes with an X/Y coordinate on the tissue. The data therefore has a shape that ordinary microbiome data does not: microsample ── community composition (which genomes, how much of each) │ ├───────── position in the tissue (X, Y, distance to the gut wall) └───────── sequencing metrics (depth, diversity) genome ── taxonomy, genome size, phylogeny, metabolic capacity This practical works through the analysis that data structure makes possible, using real data from one chicken caecum and one chicken colon. 1.1 Study design (#fig:design_figure)How MSSM data is produced, from tissue to the five tables that enter the analysis. Steps 1, 2 and 4 are what you would expect. Step 3 is not, and the next section explains why it matters more than it looks. 1.2 The question Bacteria in the gut are not randomly mixed. Communities a few hundred micrometres apart differ, and they differ systematically — along gradients that run from the gut wall out into the lumen. Can we detect such a gradient, and can we say which kind of bacteria sit at each end of it? Answering it takes four steps, one per chapter: Chapter Question Method 2 What does a microsample community actually look like? Coverage filtering, genome counts, Hill numbers 3 Is there any spatial structure, or is it noise? Tissue maps, CLR + PCA, PERMANOVA, Moran’s I 4 What explains the structure? Extended RLQ (space + environment + traits + phylogeny) 5 Does it hold up? Exercises: null models, replication, parameter choices 1.3 The data Everything you need is in this repository — nothing to download. Object What it is sample_metadata 336 microsamples: coordinates, distance to gut wall, sequencing depth genome_read_counts Reads mapped to each of 223 genomes in each microsample genome_covered_bases How much of each genome those reads actually covered genome_metadata Taxonomy, genome length, completeness of each genome genome_tree Phylogeny of the 223 genomes genome_gifts Metabolic capacity of each genome (GIFT scores) The 223 genomes are metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) built beforehand from conventional, macro-scale sequencing of the same animals. Microsample reads are mapped against that catalogue — a microsample on its own has far too little DNA to assemble anything. Two cryosections are included, chosen so you can compare gut regions: Cryosection Region Microsamples G121eI117A Caecum 168 G121eO306A Colon 168 Both come from the same animal (G121), so differences between them are about gut region and not about which chicken they came from. 1.3.1 A deliberately unnormalised protocol One design decision shapes every analysis in this book, and it is worth understanding before you touch the data. In conventional metagenomics, each library is quantified after preparation and pooled equimolarly, so that every sample receives roughly the same number of reads. Sequencing depth is then a technical nuisance, deliberately equalised, and any residual variation in it is something to correct for. MSSM does the opposite: every microsample is cut to the same area, so the same amount of tissue enters each library; every library gets the same number of PCR cycles, so amplification does not rescale anything; libraries are pooled without normalisation; all libraries from one cryosection are sequenced in a single run. The consequence is that the reads a microsample receives are roughly proportional to the DNA that went into it — and therefore to the microbial biomass it contained. Depth stops being a nuisance and becomes a quasi-quantitative measurement that equimolar pooling would have destroyed. Two caveats come with it, and both matter later: It is relative, not absolute. One run is shared out among the microsamples of one cryosection, so a microsample’s depth is its share of that cryosection’s total biomass. The composition closes at the cryosection level, and depths are not comparable between cryosections or runs. This is why every analysis in Chapters 3 and 4 is done within a single section. It is a proxy, not a calibrated measurement. Extraction efficiency, library quality and PCR stochasticity vary too. And because deeper sequencing detects more genomes, anything computed from depth — richness above all — inherits both the biological signal and the detection effect. Read this as an unusual choice, not an oversight. For most metagenomics, unnormalised pooling would be a mistake: it wastes reads on samples that do not need them and starves those that do. For MSSM it is the point. Biomass varies enormously between neighbouring pieces of tissue, that variation is part of the spatial biology being studied, and equimolar pooling would erase it. This is a simplified version. The practical was extracted from the repository that accompanies the manuscript and cut down to what fits a course session. The published study also validated the method against FISH microscopy and conventional metagenomics, compared genome catalogues, quantified contamination, and analysed strain-level variation. None of that is here. The original, full analysis lives at github.com/3d-omics/MSSM. 1.4 The study behind it The data and the analysis come from: Carlotta Pietroni†, Bryan Wang†, Amalia Bogri†, Jorge Langa, Iñaki Odriozola, Zoé Horisberger, Marta Contreras-Serrano, Jonas Greve Lauritsen, Nanna Gaun, Amalia Toffano, Anders Miki Bojesen, Ida Thøfner, Victoria Drauch, Jaime Ramirez Cerrillos, Søren Johannes Sørensen, Urvish Trivedi*, Antton Alberdi*. Chapter 2 What a microsample looks like Before any spatial analysis, we need a community table we can trust. This chapter builds one from raw mapping output and shows why micro-scale data needs a filtering step that ordinary metagenomics can skip. 2.1 The raw tables Reads from each microsample were mapped against the catalogue of 223 genomes. That produces two tables of exactly the same shape. # how many reads from each microsample mapped to each genome genome_read_counts[1:5, 1:4] # A tibble: 5 × 4 genome M306662 M306663 M306664 <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 D300418:bin_000001 284 1833 952 2 D300418:bin_000013 70 189 160 3 D300428:bin_000008 54 557 321 4 D300430:bin_000010 18507 100593 76089 5 D300432:bin_000001 210 1441 861 # how many bases of each genome those reads covered genome_covered_bases[1:5, 1:4] # A tibble: 5 × 4 genome M306662 M306663 M306664 <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 D300418:bin_000001 13008 13910 17974 2 D300418:bin_000013 2573 3754 4827 3 D300428:bin_000008 4385 19153 15907 4 D300430:bin_000010 1067323 2259902 2364991 5 D300432:bin_000001 8428 12083 12304 dim(genome_read_counts) # genomes x (1 + microsamples) [1] 223 337 And a table describing the microsamples themselves: sample_metadata %>% select(microsample, cryosection, region, Xcoord, Ycoord, distance_host, after_filtering.total_bases) %>% head() # A tibble: 6 × 7 microsample cryosection region Xcoord Ycoord distance_host <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 M306662 G121eO306A Colon 39437. 18262. 233. 2 M306663 G121eO306A Colon 39668. 18540. 448. 3 M306664 G121eO306A Colon 39839. 18989. 562. 4 M306666 G121eO306A Colon 39567. 19394. 262. 5 M306667 G121eO306A Colon 39610. 19673. 213. 6 M306668 G121eO306A Colon 40115. 19732. 642. # ℹ 1 more variable: after_filtering.total_bases <dbl> Xcoord and Ycoord are the position of the microsample on the cryosection in micrometres. distance_host is how far it sits from the epithelium — the gut wall — which is the gradient we will eventually be testing against. Scale check. A microsample covers a few hundred micrometres. The whole cryosection is a couple of millimetres across. The 168 microsamples of one section together weigh less than a grain of salt. 2.2 Sequencing depth is data here, not a nuisance The introduction described the unnormalised pooling protocol. You can verify it in the metadata: every microsample was cut to the same area and given the same number of PCR cycles. sample_metadata %>% count(cryosection, size, cycles, name = "microsamples") # A tibble: 2 × 4 cryosection size cycles microsamples <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int> 1 G121eI117A 5000 15 168 2 G121eO306A 5000 15 168 Identical input area, identical amplification, no equimolar normalisation. So how much do the resulting library sizes differ? sample_metadata %>% group_by(cryosection) %>% summarise( total_Gb = round(sum(after_filtering.total_bases) / 1e9, 1), min_Mb = round(min(after_filtering.total_bases) / 1e6, 1), median_Mb = round(median(after_filtering.total_bases) / 1e6, 1), max_Mb = round(max(after_filtering.total_bases) / 1e6, 1), fold_range = round(max(after_filtering.total_bases) / min(after_filtering.total_bases)), .groups = "drop" ) # A tibble: 2 × 6 cryosection total_Gb min_Mb median_Mb max_Mb fold_range <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 G121eI117A 1040. 43.5 5671. 18221. 419 2 G121eO306A 749. 23.1 3744. 31585. 1366 A 400- to 1,400-fold spread, between pieces of tissue of identical size processed identically. Under equimolar pooling this range would have been flattened to near-uniform by design. Here it survives, and the most plausible thing it reflects is how much microbial biomass each microsample contained. ggplot(sample_metadata, aes(x = after_filtering.total_bases, fill = region)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.85, position = "identity") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = " Mb")) + scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors) + labs(x = "Sequenced bases per microsample (log scale)", y = "Microsamples", fill = "Region") Keep this in mind for the rest of the practical. When sequencing depth turns up as a strong predictor in Chapter 3, the reflex from ordinary metagenomics — that is a technical artefact, control for it — is the wrong reflex. Under this protocol it is a biological quantity in disguise. It is not a clean one, though. Depth also determines how many genomes you can possibly detect, so richness and depth are confounded by construction. We will see exactly how strongly in a moment. 2.3 Why micro-scale data needs a coverage filter Each microsample contains very little DNA, so it is sequenced shallowly. Look at how many genomes appear to be present in a typical microsample if we simply count non-zero entries: naive_present <- colSums(genome_read_counts[, -1] > 0) summary(naive_present) Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 168.0 221.0 222.0 220.2 222.0 223.0 Almost every genome in the catalogue picks up some reads in some microsample. That cannot all be real. Short read mapping is a heuristic: a read from a genome that is genuinely present will also align, imperfectly, to its relatives. Those stray reads land scattered across the wrong genome. That scattering is what lets us tell the two cases apart. A genome that is really there gets covered evenly along its length; a genome that only catches stray reads gets a few isolated patches. So instead of asking how many reads, we ask how much of the genome was covered. genome_coverage <- breadth_of_coverage(genome_covered_bases, genome_metadata) genome_coverage[1:5, 1:4] # A tibble: 5 × 4 genome M306662 M306663 M306664 <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 D300418:bin_000001 0.00726 0.00777 0.0100 2 D300418:bin_000013 0.00110 0.00161 0.00207 3 D300428:bin_000008 0.00228 0.00996 0.00827 4 D300430:bin_000010 0.356 0.753 0.788 5 D300432:bin_000001 0.00302 0.00432 0.00440 coverage_long <- genome_coverage %>% pivot_longer(-genome, names_to = "microsample", values_to = "coverage") %>% filter(coverage > 0) ggplot(coverage_long, aes(x = coverage)) + geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#4a6ab7", colour = NA) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#E76F51", linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("text", x = 0.33, y = Inf, label = " 0.3 threshold", hjust = 0, vjust = 2, colour = "#E76F51", size = 3.5) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Fraction of genome length covered", y = "Genome × microsample pairs (log scale)", title = "Breadth of coverage is strongly bimodal") The distribution has two humps: a large one near zero (genomes catching a handful of stray reads) and a smaller one at high coverage (genomes genuinely present). Almost nothing sits in between, which is what makes a threshold defensible. We use 0.3, as in the published analysis. 2.4 Filtering and normalising Two operations turn the raw table into a community table. Coverage filtering zeroes out any genome–microsample pair below the threshold: read_counts_filt <- filter_by_coverage(genome_read_counts, genome_coverage, min_coverage = 0.3) tibble( step = c("before filtering", "after filtering"), nonzero_entries = c(sum(genome_read_counts[, -1] > 0), sum(read_counts_filt[, -1] > 0)), reads_kept_pct = c(100, round(100 * sum(read_counts_filt[, -1]) / sum(genome_read_counts[, -1]), 1)) ) # A tibble: 2 × 3 step nonzero_entries reads_kept_pct <chr> <int> <dbl> 1 before filtering 73991 100 2 after filtering 22263 92.6 Note what happened: most entries are discarded, but almost all reads are kept. The filter removes a huge number of near-empty cells that were carrying very little signal. Length normalisation converts read counts into genome counts. A 6 Mb genome captures twice as many reads as a 3 Mb genome at equal abundance, so we divide by genome length expressed in reads: genome_counts <- to_genome_counts(read_counts_filt, genome_metadata, read_length = 150) genome_counts[1:5, 1:4] # A tibble: 5 × 4 genome M306662 M306663 M306664 <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 D300418:bin_000001 0 0 0 2 D300418:bin_000013 0 0 0 3 D300428:bin_000008 0 0 0 4 D300430:bin_000010 0.925 5.03 3.80 5 D300432:bin_000001 0 0 0 Why not rarefy? Rarefying subsamples every microsample down to a common depth. That would throw away exactly the quantity this protocol went to trouble to preserve — the depth differences that track biomass — and it would still leave the within-microsample counts compositional. Chapter 3 instead splits the problem in two: a log-ratio transformation for what the community is made of, and depth kept as its own variable for how much of it there was. 2.5 Diversity per microsample With a community table we can ask how diverse each microsample is. We use Hill numbers, which put richness and evenness on the same scale (effective number of genomes): diversity <- alpha_diversity(genome_counts, genome_tree) sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(diversity, by = "microsample") sample_metadata %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise( microsamples = n(), richness = median(richness), neutral = round(median(neutral), 1), phylogenetic = round(median(phylogenetic), 1), .groups = "drop" ) # A tibble: 2 × 5 region microsamples richness neutral phylogenetic <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 Caecum 168 76 37.1 3.9 2 Colon 168 68.5 35.1 3.8 Metric q Reads as richness 0 how many genomes are present neutral 1 how many genomes are effectively present, weighting by abundance phylogenetic 1 same, but close relatives count as partly redundant Richness far above neutral diversity means a microsample is dominated by a few genomes with a long rare tail — which is exactly what these communities look like. And here is the confounding promised above: sample_metadata %>% filter(richness > 0) %>% ggplot(aes(x = after_filtering.total_bases, y = richness, colour = region)) + geom_point(size = 1.3, alpha = 0.75) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = " Mb")) + scale_colour_manual(values = region_colors) + labs(x = "Sequenced bases (log scale)", y = "Richness", colour = "Region") sample_metadata %>% filter(richness > 0) %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(spearman_rho = round(cor(richness, log(after_filtering.total_bases), method = "spearman"), 2), .groups = "drop") # A tibble: 2 × 2 region spearman_rho <chr> <dbl> 1 Caecum 0.94 2 Colon 0.93 ρ above 0.9. Two mechanisms produce that, and this dataset cannot separate them: a microsample with more biomass genuinely holds more genomes, and a microsample sequenced more deeply detects more of whatever it holds. Both are real; neither can be switched off. Any claim resting on richness alone in this kind of data is on thin ice. sample_metadata %>% pivot_longer(c(richness, neutral, phylogenetic), names_to = "metric", values_to = "diversity") %>% mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = c("richness", "neutral", "phylogenetic"))) %>% ggplot(aes(x = region, y = diversity, fill = region)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, width = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) + facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") + scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors, guide = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Diversity (effective number of genomes)") 2.6 Who is actually there composition <- genome_counts %>% pivot_longer(-genome, names_to = "microsample", values_to = "count") %>% group_by(microsample) %>% mutate(rel = count / sum(count)) %>% ungroup() %>% left_join(genome_metadata %>% select(genome, phylum, order), by = "genome") %>% left_join(sample_metadata %>% select(microsample, region, distance_host), by = "microsample") %>% filter(rel > 0) composition %>% # order microsamples by distance to the gut wall, the gradient of interest mutate(microsample = fct_reorder(microsample, distance_host)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = microsample, y = rel, fill = order)) + geom_col(width = 1) + facet_grid(~ region, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") + scale_fill_manual(values = order_colors) + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + labs(x = "Microsample (ordered by distance to gut wall →)", y = "Relative abundance", fill = "Order") + theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), legend.key.size = unit(0.35, "cm"), legend.text = element_text(size = 7)) Two things are already visible, and they set up the rest of the practical: Caecum and colon are different communities. No surprise — they are different organs. Within each section, neighbouring bars resemble each other. Microsamples are sorted here by distance to the gut wall, and the composition does not look randomly shuffled along that axis. Point 2 is a hint, not evidence. A barplot sorted by a variable will always look somewhat ordered. Chapter 3 tests it properly.

Chapter 3 Is the community spatially structured? Chapter 2 produced a community table. This chapter asks the question that makes the data worth collecting: do nearby microsamples host more similar communities than distant ones? We will attack it with the standard microbial ecology toolkit — ordination, PERMANOVA, spatial autocorrelation — and that toolkit will mostly fail. Understanding why it fails is the point of this chapter, and the reason Chapter 4 needs a different method. 3.1 Putting the microsamples back on the tissue The most direct thing to do with spatial data is look at it. Every microsample has a pixel position on the photograph of its cryosection, so any per-microsample number can be painted onto the tissue. plot_on_section("G121eI117A", sample_metadata, "richness", "Richness", pixel_coords, diverging = FALSE) + plot_on_section("G121eO306A", sample_metadata, "richness", "Richness", pixel_coords, diverging = FALSE) And the variable we ultimately care about — how far each microsample sits from the epithelium, the living gut wall: plot_on_section("G121eI117A", sample_metadata, "distance_host", "Distance to\ngut wall (µm)", pixel_coords, diverging = FALSE) + plot_on_section("G121eO306A", sample_metadata, "distance_host", "Distance to\ngut wall (µm)", pixel_coords, diverging = FALSE) Distance to the wall varies smoothly across the section — it is a genuine spatial gradient, by construction. Richness looks patchier. Whether those patches mean anything is what the rest of the chapter tests. 3.2 Compositional data and the CLR transformation We now have to separate two questions that the raw table mixes together: how much was in a microsample, and what it was made of. The first is sequencing depth, which under this protocol carries biomass information (Chapter 2). We set it aside deliberately here and pick it up again as its own variable. The second is composition, and it is genuinely compositional: within a microsample, only the ratios between genomes are interpretable. Euclidean distances on raw proportions are misleading, and the standard fix is the centred log-ratio (CLR) — divide every value by the geometric mean of its microsample, then take logs. Note what CLR does to the total: it divides it out entirely. That is the right move for asking what lives here, and it is exactly why the biomass signal has to be reintroduced separately later. Logs need positive numbers, so zeros are replaced first, using a Bayesian estimator that respects the compositional structure. comm_all <- genome_counts %>% column_to_rownames("genome") %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() comm_all <- comm_all[rowSums(comm_all) > 0, colSums(comm_all) > 0, drop = FALSE] # zeros -> small positive values; genomes too sparse to estimate are dropped comm_repl <- cmultRepl(comm_all, method = "GBM", output = "prop", z.warning = 0.95) No. adjusted imputations: 1569 clr <- function(x) log(x) - rowMeans(log(x)) comm_clr <- clr(as.matrix(comm_repl)) dim(comm_clr) # microsamples x genomes retained [1] 324 89 Note how much shrank: from 223 genomes to under a hundred. Everything else was too sparse across these two cryosections to place on a log scale at all. pca <- prcomp(comm_clr, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE) var_pct <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1) pca_scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2]) %>% rownames_to_column("microsample") %>% left_join(sample_metadata, by = "microsample") ggplot(pca_scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = region)) + geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) + stat_ellipse(linewidth = 0.5) + scale_colour_manual(values = region_colors) + labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pct[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pct[2], "%)"), colour = "Region") The two organs overlap heavily. Let us quantify that with PERMANOVA, which asks whether a variable explains more between-sample distance than label shuffling would produce by chance. dist_clr <- dist(comm_clr, method = "euclidean") # Aitchison distance meta_ord <- sample_metadata %>% filter(microsample %in% rownames(comm_clr)) %>% arrange(match(microsample, rownames(comm_clr))) adonis2(dist_clr ~ region, data = meta_ord, permutations = 999) Permutation test for adonis under reduced model Permutation: free Number of permutations: 999 adonis2(formula = dist_clr ~ region, data = meta_ord, permutations = 999) Df SumOfSqs R2 F Pr(>F) Model 1 363.4 0.03142 10.447 0.001 *** Residual 322 11201.1 0.96858 Total 323 11564.5 1.00000 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Caecum and colon differ significantly — but R² is only about 3%. Two different organs, and the difference between them accounts for a thirtieth of the variation in the data. First real result. At this scale, variation between neighbouring microsamples within one section dwarfs the variation between gut regions. That is the whole justification for micro-scale sampling: homogenise a caecum and you average away 97% of what is actually going on. 3.3 Working within a single cryosection If local variation is where the signal is, the analysis belongs inside one cryosection, where gut region, animal, and laboratory batch are all held constant and the only thing that varies is position. prepare_section() does that: it pulls out one section, drops empty microsamples, and replaces zeros within that section alone. caecum <- prepare_section("G121eI117A", genome_counts, sample_metadata) No. adjusted imputations: 457 colon <- prepare_section("G121eO306A", genome_counts, sample_metadata) No. adjusted imputations: 1006 tibble( section = c(caecum$section, colon$section), microsamples = c(nrow(caecum$comm_red), nrow(colon$comm_red)), genomes = c(ncol(caecum$comm_red), ncol(colon$comm_red)) ) # A tibble: 2 × 3 section microsamples genomes <chr> <int> <int> 1 G121eI117A 165 92 2 G121eO306A 159 87 Now the key test. Does distance to the gut wall explain community composition inside a single 2 mm section? caecum_clr <- clr(as.matrix(caecum$comm_zero_repl)) caecum_dist <- dist(caecum_clr) caecum_meta <- caecum$metadata adonis2(caecum_dist ~ distance_host, data = caecum_meta, permutations = 999) Permutation test for adonis under reduced model Permutation: free Number of permutations: 999 adonis2(formula = caecum_dist ~ distance_host, data = caecum_meta, permutations = 999) Df SumOfSqs R2 F Pr(>F) Model 1 47.2 0.00872 1.4335 0.09 . Residual 163 5364.1 0.99128 Total 164 5411.3 1.00000 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Not significant. Now compare that with the coordinates themselves, and with sequencing depth — in both sections: colon_clr <- clr(as.matrix(colon$comm_zero_repl)) colon_dist <- dist(colon_clr) colon_meta <- colon$metadata permanova_row <- function(dist_matrix, meta, rhs, label, section) { a <- adonis2(as.formula(paste("dist_matrix ~", rhs)), data = meta, permutations = 999) tibble(section = section, term = label, R2 = round(a$R2[1], 4), F = round(a$F[1], 2), p = a$`Pr(>F)`[1]) } terms <- list( c("distance_host", "distance to gut wall"), c("Xcoord + Ycoord", "X + Y coordinates"), c("log(after_filtering.total_bases)", "log(sequencing depth)") ) bind_rows( map_dfr(terms, ~ permanova_row(caecum_dist, caecum_meta, .x[1], .x[2], "caecum")), map_dfr(terms, ~ permanova_row(colon_dist, colon_meta, .x[1], .x[2], "colon")) ) # A tibble: 6 × 5 section term R2 F p <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 caecum distance to gut wall 0.0087 1.43 0.076 2 caecum X + Y coordinates 0.0216 1.78 0.005 3 caecum log(sequencing depth) 0.0508 8.73 0.001 4 colon distance to gut wall 0.007 1.11 0.277 5 colon X + Y coordinates 0.0169 1.34 0.096 6 colon log(sequencing depth) 0.115 20.3 0.001 Permutation p-values wobble. PERMANOVA estimates significance by shuffling, so re-running the same test gives slightly different p-values (0.08 rather than 0.09, say). Read them as approximate, and never as a hard threshold. Sequencing depth is by far the strongest predictor of community composition, in both sections — five to eleven times more explanatory than distance to the gut wall. In an equimolar-pooled study this would be a red flag: a technical variable driving composition means something went wrong. Here it is not. Depth stands in for biomass, and it is entirely reasonable that microsamples holding more bacteria hold a different community from microsamples holding very few. Dense and sparse patches of gut content are different habitats. What the result does mean is that biomass, not position, is the leading axis of compositional variation inside a cryosection. Any spatial gradient we hope to find has to be looked for underneath it. 3.4 Spatial autocorrelation To measure spatial structure directly we need a definition of “nearby”. Microsamples are not on a regular grid — the laser cuts where the tissue allows — so rather than pick a distance cutoff we build a Gabriel graph: two microsamples are joined when no third one lies inside the circle having them as its diameter. caecum_nb <- neighbour_graph(caecum_meta[, c("Xcoord", "Ycoord")]) caecum_nb Neighbour list object: Number of regions: 165 Number of nonzero links: 698 Percentage nonzero weights: 2.56382 Average number of links: 4.230303 plot_neighbour_graph(caecum_meta[, c("Xcoord", "Ycoord")], caecum_nb, point_values = caecum_meta$richness, value_label = "Richness") + labs(title = "Gabriel neighbour graph, caecum section G121eI117A") Moran’s I is a correlation coefficient for space: it compares each microsample’s value with its neighbours’. I > 0 — neighbours resemble each other (spatial structure) I ≈ 0 — values arranged at random I < 0 — neighbours systematically unlike each other Computing it at increasing lag orders — direct neighbours, then neighbours-of-neighbours, and so on — shows how far the resemblance reaches. correlograms <- bind_rows( moran_correlogram(caecum_nb, log(caecum_meta$distance_host)) %>% mutate(variable = "log(distance to gut wall)"), moran_correlogram(caecum_nb, log(caecum_meta$after_filtering.total_bases)) %>% mutate(variable = "log(sequencing depth)"), moran_correlogram(caecum_nb, log(caecum_meta$richness)) %>% mutate(variable = "log(richness)"), moran_correlogram(caecum_nb, prcomp(caecum_clr)$x[, 1]) %>% mutate(variable = "composition (CLR-PCA axis 1)") ) %>% mutate(variable = fct_inorder(variable)) ggplot(correlograms, aes(x = lag, y = morans_i)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#4a6ab7", alpha = 0.2) + geom_line(colour = "#4a6ab7") + geom_point(colour = "#4a6ab7", size = 1.8) + facet_wrap(~ variable, nrow = 1) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 8, 2)) + labs(x = "Lag order (steps through the neighbour graph)", y = "Moran's I") Read the four panels in order: Distance to the gut wall is strongly autocorrelated at short lags and turns negative at long ones — the signature of a gradient. This is guaranteed: it is a smooth function of position. Sequencing depth is also autocorrelated, weakly but clearly (I = 0.14, p = 0.003). Read as biomass, this is a result in its own right: microbial biomass is spatially patchy at the sub-millimetre scale. Neighbouring pieces of tissue tend to be densely or sparsely colonised together. Richness is essentially flat — despite correlating with depth at ρ > 0.9. Worth pausing on: two variables can be tightly correlated and still differ in spatial behaviour. Composition, summarised as the first CLR-PCA axis, is also flat. lw <- nb2listw(caecum_nb) map_dfr( list( "log(distance to gut wall)" = log(caecum_meta$distance_host), "log(sequencing depth)" = log(caecum_meta$after_filtering.total_bases), "log(richness)" = log(caecum_meta$richness), "composition (PCA axis 1)" = prcomp(caecum_clr)$x[, 1] ), function(v) { tst <- moran.test(v, lw, zero.policy = TRUE) tibble(morans_i = round(unname(tst$estimate[1]), 3), p_value = signif(tst$p.value, 3)) }, .id = "variable" ) # A tibble: 4 × 3 variable morans_i p_value <chr> <dbl> <dbl> 1 log(distance to gut wall) 0.56 1.22e-25 2 log(sequencing depth) 0.14 3.31e- 3 3 log(richness) 0.01 3.75e- 1 4 composition (PCA axis 1) 0.001 4.47e- 1 3.5 Why the obvious approach failed By the standard toolkit, this dataset has no spatial structure in community composition. But that conclusion rests entirely on one choice we never examined: using PCA axis 1 as the summary of “what lives here”. PCA ranks its axes by variance, not by relevance. Nothing guarantees that the largest axis is the interesting one. Look at what the first three axes actually correspond to: caecum_pca <- prcomp(caecum_clr) caecum_var <- round(100 * caecum_pca$sdev^2 / sum(caecum_pca$sdev^2), 1) map_dfr(1:3, function(k) { ax <- caecum_pca$x[, k] tst <- moran.test(ax, lw, zero.policy = TRUE) tibble( axis = paste0("PC", k), variance_pct = caecum_var[k], rho_depth = round(cor(ax, log(caecum_meta$after_filtering.total_bases), method = "spearman"), 2), rho_host_dist = round(cor(ax, log(caecum_meta$distance_host), method = "spearman"), 2), morans_i = round(unname(tst$estimate[1]), 3), moran_p = signif(tst$p.value, 3) ) }) # A tibble: 3 × 6 axis variance_pct rho_depth rho_host_dist morans_i moran_p <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 PC1 13.4 -0.14 0.1 0.001 0.447 2 PC2 8.2 0.77 0.02 0.184 0.000233 3 PC3 6.4 0.02 0.21 0.146 0.00231 Read that table carefully — it is the turning point of the practical. PC1 is the biggest axis (13% of variance) and corresponds to nothing we measured: not depth, not position, and it is not spatially autocorrelated. It is unstructured microsample-to-microsample turnover — the stochastic part of who happens to be where. PC2 is the biomass axis (ρ ≈ 0.8 with depth) and is spatially autocorrelated, consistent with the patchiness we saw above. PC3 carries the weak trace of distance to the gut wall (ρ ≈ 0.2) and is also significantly autocorrelated. The gradient we came for is on axis 3. It was never going to be found by looking at axis 1, and it is smeared thinly across several axes rather than isolated on any of them — because nothing in PCA’s objective function has any reason to isolate it. What we need instead is a method that does not rank axes by size, but looks for the axis that is simultaneously organised in space and associated with the kind of bacteria involved — their metabolism and their evolutionary history. Sequencing noise cannot fake that combination: there is no reason for a microsample’s biomass to correlate with what its bacteria can metabolise. That is exactly what extended RLQ does, and it is the subject of Chapter 4.

Chapter 4 Extended RLQ: finding the gradient Chapter 3 ended in a dead end. Ordinary ordination found no spatial structure in composition, because it ranks axes by size and the gradient we wanted turned out to be axis 3 — smeared thinly, below a biomass axis and below a large axis of unstructured turnover. The fix is to stop asking for the axis with the most variance and start asking for the axis with the most covariance between two sides of the data: what we know about each microsample — where it is, how deep it was sequenced, how diverse it is; what we know about each genome — its metabolic capacity and its position in the bacterial phylogeny. An axis that scores highly on both is one where position in the tissue and kind of bacterium line up. That is precisely what a spatial gradient is, and neither noise nor biomass can fake it: there is no reason for a microsample’s DNA yield to correlate with what its bacteria can metabolise. No. adjusted imputations: 457 No. adjusted imputations: 1006 4.1 The five tables Classical RLQ analysis links three tables: environmental variables of the sites (R), the community table (L), and species traits (Q). It finds the axes along which R and Q covary through L. Extended RLQ (Pavoine et al. 2011) adds two more: the spatial arrangement of the sites (S) and the phylogeny of the species (P). Five tables, hence ESLTP. Table In this dataset Rows E environment sequencing depth (≈ biomass), richness, distance to gut wall microsamples S space Gabriel-graph neighbourhood structure microsamples L community Hellinger-transformed genome abundances microsamples × genomes T traits metabolic capacity (GIFT), ordinated genomes P phylogeny patristic distances on the MAG tree genomes 4.1.1 Traits: what can each genome do? Genome traits come from GIFTs (genome-inferred functional traits): for each genome, the completeness of every metabolic pathway it encodes, from its annotated genes. Nearly 300 traits per genome is too many to feed to RLQ directly, so we ordinate them first and keep the two main axes of metabolic variation. # genomes that survived filtering in either section genomes_used <- union(colnames(caecum$comm_red), colnames(colon$comm_red)) gifts_used <- genome_gifts[rownames(genome_gifts) %in% genomes_used, !grepl("^S0|^D04", colnames(genome_gifts)), drop = FALSE] dim(gifts_used) # genomes x metabolic traits [1] 92 292 trait_pcoa <- ape::pcoa(dist(gifts_used)) round(trait_pcoa$values$Relative_eig[1:5], 3) [1] 0.138 0.094 0.071 0.052 0.045 A shared trait ordination is used for both sections, so that an axis means the same thing in the caecum and in the colon. as.data.frame(trait_pcoa$vectors[, 1:2]) %>% rownames_to_column("genome") %>% left_join(genome_metadata, by = "genome") %>% ggplot(aes(Axis.1, Axis.2, colour = order, size = length / 1e6)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.9) + scale_colour_manual(values = order_colors) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.8, 5), name = "Genome size (Mb)") + guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) + labs(x = "Metabolic PCoA 1", y = "Metabolic PCoA 2", title = "Metabolic trait space of the genomes") Bacterial orders occupy distinct parts of trait space, and genome size varies across it — related bacteria have similar metabolic repertoires. This is why the phylogeny table P is worth including separately: it captures the part of “what kind of bacterium” that the trait table misses. 4.2 Running the analysis rlq_caecum <- spatial_rlq("G121eI117A", caecum$comm_red, caecum$metadata, trait_pcoa, genome_tree) rlq_colon <- spatial_rlq("G121eO306A", colon$comm_red, colon$metadata, trait_pcoa, genome_tree) round(rlq_caecum$eig_prop[1:4], 3) # share of co-inertia per axis [1] 0.717 0.140 0.032 0.027 Two axes carry almost everything. Their sign is arbitrary — flipping an axis changes nothing but which end is drawn red — so we fix a convention that makes the caecum figures read left to right: rlq_caecum <- flip_rlq_axes(rlq_caecum, axes = c(1, 2)) caecum_sites <- rlq_site_scores(rlq_caecum, caecum$metadata) caecum_genomes <- rlq_genome_scores(rlq_caecum, genome_metadata) colon_sites <- rlq_site_scores(rlq_colon, colon$metadata) colon_genomes <- rlq_genome_scores(rlq_colon, genome_metadata) head(caecum_sites %>% select(microsample, axis1, axis2, distance_host)) # A tibble: 6 × 4 microsample axis1 axis2 distance_host <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> 1 M306710 -5.48 0.467 599. 2 M306711 -2.76 1.61 482. 3 M306712 -0.461 -0.0186 630. 4 M306714 -0.878 1.26 337. 5 M306715 0.256 0.109 492. 6 M306716 -0.0324 0.418 212. Every microsample now has two coordinates in RLQ space, and so does every genome. That is the whole point of the method: microsamples and genomes are placed on the same axes. 4.3 What is each axis? Never interpret an RLQ axis before checking what drives it. Correlate both axes against every microsample variable that went into E: axis_correlations <- function(sites, label) { vars <- list( "distance to gut wall" = log(sites$distance_host), "sequencing depth" = log(sites$after_filtering.total_bases), "richness" = sites$richness ) map_dfr(names(vars), function(v) { tibble(section = label, variable = v, axis1 = round(cor(sites$axis1, vars[[v]], method = "spearman"), 2), axis2 = round(cor(sites$axis2, vars[[v]], method = "spearman"), 2)) }) } bind_rows(axis_correlations(caecum_sites, "caecum"), axis_correlations(colon_sites, "colon")) # A tibble: 6 × 4 section variable axis1 axis2 <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> 1 caecum distance to gut wall -0.11 0.48 2 caecum sequencing depth 0.93 -0.3 3 caecum richness 0.95 -0.37 4 colon distance to gut wall -0.03 0.01 5 colon sequencing depth 0.94 0.6 6 colon richness 0.94 0.65 This table is the crux of the whole practical. Axis 1 is sequencing depth and richness, in both sections (|ρ| ≈ 0.9). It is the biomass axis. Because libraries were pooled without normalisation (see the introduction), depth stands in for how much microbial biomass a microsample held, and axis 1 says that this is the dominant organising gradient of MSSM data. RLQ has separated it onto an axis of its own, which is what lets axis 2 be read cleanly. Caecum axis 2 correlates with distance to the gut wall (ρ ≈ 0.5) and much more weakly with depth. This is the biological gradient. Colon axis 2 is flat against distance to the gut wall (ρ ≈ 0.01) and still partly tracks depth and richness. This section has no detectable spatial gradient — an honest negative result, and a reminder that not every cryosection has one. Is caecum axis 2 spatially autocorrelated, where PC1 was not? map_dfr( list( "caecum axis 1" = list(rlq_caecum, caecum_sites$axis1), "caecum axis 2" = list(rlq_caecum, caecum_sites$axis2), "colon axis 1" = list(rlq_colon, colon_sites$axis1), "colon axis 2" = list(rlq_colon, colon_sites$axis2) ), function(x) { tst <- moran.test(x[[2]], nb2listw(x[[1]]$nb), zero.policy = TRUE) tibble(morans_i = round(unname(tst$estimate[1]), 3), p_value = signif(tst$p.value, 3)) }, .id = "axis" ) # A tibble: 4 × 3 axis morans_i p_value <chr> <dbl> <dbl> 1 caecum axis 1 0.097 0.0267 2 caecum axis 2 0.166 0.000683 3 colon axis 1 0.038 0.214 4 colon axis 2 0.021 0.312 Caecum axis 2 is significantly autocorrelated in space, and more strongly than anything PCA produced. The signal was there all along, in a minor axis of compositional variation — minor in size, but the only one organised both spatially and functionally. Note also that axis 1, the biomass axis, is itself weakly autocorrelated (I = 0.10, p = 0.03), matching the patchiness of sequencing depth from Chapter 3. Biomass and community type are two different spatial patterns living in the same tissue, and RLQ has put them on separate axes. 4.4 The gradient on the tissue plot_on_section("G121eI117A", caecum_sites, "axis2", "Caecum\naxis 2", pixel_coords) + plot_on_section("G121eI117A", caecum_sites, "axis1", "Caecum\naxis 1", pixel_coords) Axis 2 (left) forms a coherent band running across the tissue — the gradient, made visible. Axis 1 (right) is patchier and more locally clustered, which is what a biomass map should look like: dense and sparse pockets rather than a smooth trend. caecum_sites %>% select(axis1, axis2, distance_host, after_filtering.total_bases) %>% pivot_longer(c(axis1, axis2), names_to = "axis", values_to = "score") %>% pivot_longer(c(distance_host, after_filtering.total_bases), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(variable = recode(variable, distance_host = "Distance to gut wall (µm)", after_filtering.total_bases = "Sequencing depth (bases)")) %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = score)) + geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7, colour = "grey30") + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#ba2760", fill = "#ba2760", alpha = 0.15) + facet_grid(axis ~ variable, scales = "free") + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = NULL, y = "RLQ score") Each axis responds to its own driver and is comparatively flat against the other’s. That separation is what RLQ was asked to find, and it is why the two can be interpreted independently: axis 1 is about how much, axis 2 about which. 4.5 Which bacteria sit at each end? Because genomes live on the same axes, we can ask what distinguishes the two ends of the caecum gradient. First, taxonomically: caecum_genomes %>% add_count(order) %>% filter(n >= 2) %>% mutate(order = fct_reorder(order, axis2)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = axis2, y = order, colour = order)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") + geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) + stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 124, size = 8, colour = "grey20") + scale_colour_manual(values = order_colors, guide = "none") + labs(x = "Caecum axis 2 (gut wall → lumen)", y = NULL) Then by what those genomes can do. GIFT traits are grouped into broad functions, of which the degradation functions are the biologically interesting ones here: gift_functions <- gifts_used %>% to.elements(GIFT_db_df) %>% to.functions(GIFT_db_df) %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column("genome") caecum_traits <- caecum_genomes %>% left_join(gift_functions, by = "genome") %>% mutate(genome_size_mb = length / 1e6, carb_minus_lipid = D02 - D01) caecum_traits %>% select(axis2, `Genome size (Mb)` = genome_size_mb, `Polysaccharide degradation (D02)` = D02, `Carbohydrate − lipid degradation` = carb_minus_lipid) %>% pivot_longer(-axis2, names_to = "trait", values_to = "value") %>% ggplot(aes(x = axis2, y = value)) + geom_point(size = 1.4, alpha = 0.7, colour = "grey30") + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#2A9D8F", fill = "#2A9D8F", alpha = 0.15) + facet_wrap(~ trait, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "Caecum axis 2 (gut wall → lumen)", y = NULL) tibble( trait = c("genome size", "polysaccharide degradation (D02)", "lipid degradation (D01)", "carbohydrate − lipid"), spearman_rho = c( cor(caecum_traits$axis2, caecum_traits$genome_size_mb, method = "spearman"), cor(caecum_traits$axis2, caecum_traits$D02, method = "spearman"), cor(caecum_traits$axis2, caecum_traits$D01, method = "spearman"), cor(caecum_traits$axis2, caecum_traits$carb_minus_lipid, method = "spearman") ) %>% round(2) ) # A tibble: 4 × 2 trait spearman_rho <chr> <dbl> 1 genome size 0.42 2 polysaccharide degradation (D02) 0.75 3 lipid degradation (D01) -0.33 4 carbohydrate − lipid 0.68 4.6 The gradient on the phylogeny Finally, colour the tree by each genome’s axis-2 score. If the gradient separates whole clades rather than scattered tips, it is evolutionarily conserved — bacteria inherit where they live. caecum_tree <- keep.tip(genome_tree, caecum_genomes$genome) plot_tree_gradient(caecum_tree, caecum_genomes, "axis2", "Caecum axis 2", colours = order_colors) axis2_by_genome <- setNames(caecum_genomes$axis2, caecum_genomes$genome) phytools::phylosig(caecum_tree, axis2_by_genome[caecum_tree$tip.label], method = "K", test = TRUE) Phylogenetic signal K : 1.52486 P-value (based on 1000 randomizations) : 0.001 Blomberg’s K above 1 with a significant p-value means closely related genomes occupy the same end of the gradient more than a random walk along the tree would produce. The spatial preference is phylogenetically conserved. 4.7 What the analysis found Putting the three pieces together for caecum section G121eI117A: Near the gut wall Out in the lumen Axis 2 score low high Genome size smaller larger Metabolism relatively more lipid-oriented more polysaccharide degradation Taxa Erysipelotrichales, Lactobacillales, Coriobacteriales Lachnospirales, UBA1381 This is a biologically coherent story. Complex plant polysaccharides arrive in the lumen, and degrading them needs large gene repertoires — hence larger genomes with more carbohydrate-active machinery further from the wall. Close to the epithelium the substrates are host-derived instead, and the bacteria there are smaller and differently equipped. And it took the right method to see it. The same data, analysed by PCA and PERMANOVA in Chapter 3, put this gradient on axis 3 and reported it as non-significant. It occupies a small share of total compositional variance — it was never going to be axis 1 of anything. RLQ found it because it looked for covariance between space and biology rather than for variance alone. And the protocol made it findable. Because libraries were pooled without normalisation, biomass entered the analysis as a measured variable instead of hiding inside the composition. RLQ could give it axis 1 and hand back a clean axis 2. Under equimolar pooling the biomass differences would have been flattened away, and the variation they cause would still have been in the community table — unlabelled, unmodelled, and impossible to separate from the gradient.

Exercises marked ★ are the ones worth doing if time is short. Set 1 — The coverage filter The 0.3 breadth-of-coverage threshold was presented as a given. It is a choice. 1.1 ★ Rebuild the community table at min_coverage values of 0, 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6. For each, record how many non-zero entries survive, what fraction of reads is kept, and the median richness per microsample. map_dfr(c(0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6), function(threshold) { filtered <- filter_by_coverage(genome_read_counts, genome_coverage, threshold) counts <- to_genome_counts(filtered, genome_metadata) tibble( threshold = threshold, nonzero_entries = sum(filtered[, -1] > 0), reads_kept = sum(filtered[, -1]) / sum(genome_read_counts[, -1]), median_richness = median(colSums(counts[, -1] > 0)) ) }) 1.2 At threshold 0, richness is roughly 220 genomes per microsample — nearly the whole catalogue. Why is that not a plausible biological result for a piece of tissue a few hundred micrometres across? 1.3 Re-run the caecum RLQ (Chapter 4) using a table filtered at 0.1 and again at 0.6. Does axis 2 still correlate with distance to the gut wall? Is the conclusion robust to the threshold, or does it depend on it? Set 2 — Compositionality 2.1 Chapter 3 replaced zeros before taking logs. Try instead the common shortcut of adding a pseudocount of 1 to every value, then CLR-transform and redo the PCA. How much does the ordination change? Which genomes move most, and what do they have in common? 2.2 ★ cmultRepl() dropped genomes present in fewer than 5% of microsamples. Those are rare taxa. Argue both sides: what is lost by discarding them, and what would go wrong if we kept them? 2.3 ★ CLR divides out each microsample’s total, and Chapter 3 argued that this is why biomass has to be handed to RLQ separately. Test the claim directly: compute each microsample’s total genome count, and check whether it survives the CLR transformation in any recoverable form. totals <- rowSums(caecum$comm_red) # does anything in the CLR matrix still track the total? cor(rowSums(caecum_clr), log(totals)) # CLR rows sum to zero by construction max(abs(cor(caecum_clr, log(totals)))) # any single genome? Given the answer, would an analysis that used only CLR composition be able to detect a biomass gradient at all? Set 3 — Spatial structure 3.1 ★ The Gabriel graph was one choice of neighbourhood. Rebuild it as a k-nearest-neighbour graph and as a distance-band graph: coords <- as.matrix(caecum_meta[, c("Xcoord", "Ycoord")]) nb_gabriel <- neighbour_graph(coords) nb_knn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 4)) nb_dist <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, 400) # within 400 µm # how many links does each definition produce? map_dbl(list(nb_gabriel, nb_knn, nb_dist), ~ sum(card(.x))) Recompute Moran’s I for distance-to-gut-wall under all three. Does the conclusion depend on the neighbourhood definition? Should it? 3.2 ★ In Chapter 3, sequencing depth was spatially autocorrelated in the caecum (I = 0.14) but not in the colon (I = 0.05, n.s.). Under the unnormalised pooling protocol this reads as biomass is spatially patchy in the caecum. Give one competing explanation that is purely technical, and say what you would measure to tell them apart. 3.3 The microsamples of one cryosection were prepared in four batches (batch, 42 microsamples each). If batches were laid out spatially rather than at random, batch effects would masquerade as biomass patchiness. Check whether batch is spatially clustered on the section, and whether sequencing depth differs between batches. 3.4 ★ Repeat the shuffled-coordinates null model, but instead of shuffling freely, shuffle within bands of distance to the gut wall. What does the comparison between the two nulls tell you that either alone does not? Set 4 — RLQ 4.1 ★ Table E contained three variables: sequencing depth, richness and distance to the gut wall. Drop distance to the gut wall from spatial_rlq() and re-run the caecum analysis. Does axis 2 still recover the spatial gradient? This is the most important exercise in the practical. If the gradient survives, RLQ found it through S (the neighbourhood structure) and L alone, which means it is not an artefact of having told the method what to look for. # edit the `env` data frame inside spatial_rlq(), or copy the function and # remove the log_host_dist column, then compare: # cor(new_sites$axis2, log(new_sites$distance_host), method = "spearman") 4.2 RLQ was given the phylogeny (P) and metabolic traits (T), and Chapter 4 showed they carry overlapping information. Re-run with only one of them. Which matters more for recovering the gradient? 4.3 ★ Caecum axis 1 tracked sequencing depth almost perfectly (ρ ≈ 0.93), and the practical read that as a biomass axis rather than a technical one — because libraries were pooled without normalisation. That interpretation is an argument about protocol, not about the data in front of you. Set out what the data could show that would contradict it. Then say whether any of those checks is possible with the variables in sample_metadata, and what extra measurement would settle the question outright. 4.4 ★ The colon section showed no gradient. List three explanations that have nothing to do with the colon lacking spatial structure, and say how you would distinguish them. Set 5 — Interpretation 5.1 ★ The concluding table of Chapter 4 claims that genomes further from the gut wall are larger and better equipped for polysaccharide degradation. Genome size and polysaccharide-degradation capacity are themselves correlated — bigger genomes encode more of everything. Design an analysis that separates the two explanations. 5.2 Blomberg’s K was 1.5 (p = 0.001): spatial preference is phylogenetically conserved. Does that support the metabolic explanation, undermine it, or neither? 5.3 You have one animal and one cryosection per gut region. Write the strongest version of the criticism a reviewer would make, and state what the study would need to answer it. Set 6 — Extension 6.1 The published study analysed six cryosections — three caecum, three colon — and asked whether the same gradient reappeared in each. Describe how you would test “the same gradient” quantitatively, given that RLQ axes from separate analyses are not directly comparable (different genomes, arbitrary signs, different scaling). 6.2 Microsamples here are 5,000 µm². If you could re-run the experiment at a quarter of that area, with four times as many microsamples and the same total sequencing cost, would you? Argue it in terms of what Chapter 3 showed about sequencing depth — and remember that under unnormalised pooling the faintest microsamples receive very few reads rather than a guaranteed share. 6.3 ★ Suppose a reviewer insists you pool equimolarly, as standard practice requires. Write the paragraph you would send back. What is lost, what is gained, and is there a design that gets both? Where to go next This practical is a simplified version of the study’s original analysis, which it was extracted from. The full version — method validation against FISH microscopy and conventional metagenomics, genome-catalogue comparison, contamination assessment, strain-level microdiversity, and the six-cryosection replication — is at github.com/3d-omics/MSSM.
